subject: Science
source: Edexcel IGCSE Physics 4PH1 specification (units Physics 1-4, Y10). Existing UK-GCSE lessons in content/lessons/gcse-science/y10.json already cover Physics 1 points on distance-time and velocity-time graphs, average speed, acceleration and v² = u² + 2as, resultant force, F = ma and W = mg, stopping distance and Hooke's law, so those points are not re-taught here; this file adds vectors/scalars, terminal velocity, momentum and moments.

lessons.title: Vectors, scalars and resultant forces in two dimensions
lessons.bigQuestion: Why does a runner who completes a 400 m lap have a distance of 400 m but a displacement of zero?
objectives: Distinguish vector from scalar quantities and give SI units
Calculate the resultant of two perpendicular forces
Use a scale drawing to find a resultant
successCriteria: All: classify quantities as vector or scalar
Most: find a resultant of two perpendicular forces by Pythagoras
Some: find its direction using trigonometry or a scale drawing
lessons.crossCurricular: Maths: Pythagoras, trigonometry and scale drawing
lessons.smsc: Moral: precision in measurement and honest reporting of results

keywords.def: a quantity with magnitude (size) only
a quantity with magnitude and direction
distance in a straight line from start to finish, with direction
the single force that has the same effect as all the forces acting together

starter: Bismillah. State the SI unit of force, mass, time and energy.
A car travels 90 km in 1.5 hours. Calculate its average speed in km/h.
A 4 kg trolley has a resultant force of 12 N. Calculate its acceleration.

teach.heading: Scalars and vectors
bullets: Scalar: size only, e.g. mass, distance, speed, time, energy
Vector: size and direction, e.g. force, velocity, displacement
Vectors are drawn as arrows: length shows size
teach.note: Ask pupils to sort ten quantities onto mini-whiteboards. Recall SI base units here: metre, kilogram, second; newton (N) and joule (J) are derived units. Stress that in one dimension direction can be shown by a sign (+/-).

teach.heading: Forces at right angles
bullets: Forces that do not line up cannot simply be added
For perpendicular forces use Pythagoras: R² = F₁² + F₂²
Direction: tan θ = opposite ÷ adjacent
teach.note: Draw the force triangle head-to-tail on the board. Walk through why 6 N and 8 N do not make 14 N. Show that a scale drawing (1 cm = 1 kN) gives the same answer, as examiners may ask for either method.

model.problem: Two tugboats pull a ship. One pulls 6.0 kN due east, the other 8.0 kN due north. Find the size and direction of the resultant.
steps: Draw the forces head to tail as a right-angled triangle
tan θ = 8.0 ÷ 6.0 = 1.33, so θ = 53° north of east
model.answer: Resultant = 10 kN at 53° north of east

teach.heading: Distance and displacement
bullets: Distance is how far you travelled along the path
Displacement is the straight-line distance from the start, with direction
Speed is a scalar; velocity is a vector
teach.note: Return to the big question: a full lap gives displacement 0, so average velocity is 0 even though average speed is not. Ask: can an object move at constant speed but changing velocity? (Yes: circular motion.)

misconception.wrong: A negative velocity means the object is slowing down.
misconception.right: A negative velocity only means the direction is opposite to the one chosen as positive. Slowing down means the acceleration is opposite to the velocity.

teach.heading: Check: scalar or vector?
bullets: Decide, then show your whiteboards
teach.note: Hinge question. Pupils choosing B are thinking only of size. Pupils choosing C or D have mixed up vectors and scalars, for example thinking weight and mass are the same.

check.q: Which list contains only vector quantities?
check.why: Force, displacement and acceleration all have direction. Speed (B, D), mass, time, energy and distance are scalars.

practice: A boat is pushed 9 N east by the engine and 12 N north by the current. Calculate the size of the resultant force.
A hiker walks 3 km east then 4 km north. State her distance and her displacement.
Draw a scale diagram (1 cm = 2 N) to find the resultant of 10 N west and 4 N south.
independent: Core: Classify each as scalar or vector: temperature, momentum, volume, acceleration, speed, displacement.
Extend: Forces of 5.0 N and 12 N act at right angles on a 2.0 kg trolley. Calculate the resultant and the magnitude of the acceleration.
Stretch: A swimmer aims directly across a 60 m wide river at 1.5 m/s. The river flows at 2.0 m/s. Calculate the swimmer's resultant speed and how far downstream she lands.
exit: Explain the difference between speed and velocity.
A force of 3 N and a force of 4 N act at right angles. Show that the resultant is 5 N.
lessons.homework: Find three everyday situations where two forces act at an angle and write one sentence about each. Then complete five resultant-force calculations from the worksheet.
lessons.send: SEND: give a pre-drawn right-angled triangle template and a Pythagoras triples card (3-4-5, 5-12-13). EAL: pair 'scalar' and 'vector' with drawn arrows. Stretch: resolve a force into horizontal and vertical components.

lessons.title: Falling objects, drag and terminal velocity
lessons.bigQuestion: Why does a skydiver stop speeding up even though gravity never switches off?
objectives: Describe the forces on a falling object
Explain terminal velocity in terms of balanced forces
Interpret a velocity-time graph for a skydiver
successCriteria: All: state that terminal velocity is reached when forces balance
Most: explain each stage of a skydive using resultant force
Some: calculate acceleration at a given instant from weight and drag
lessons.crossCurricular: PE/Geography: skydiving; DT: parachute shapes
lessons.smsc: Spiritual: wonder at the laws that govern ordinary things

keywords.def: resistive force on an object moving through a fluid, such as air resistance
the constant maximum speed reached when drag equals the driving force
the force of gravity on an object, W = mg
the overall force after adding forces with direction

starter: Bismillah. Calculate the weight of a 60 kg person (g = 10 N/kg).
State Newton's second law as an equation.
Describe a velocity-time graph showing constant acceleration.

teach.heading: Two forces on a falling object
bullets: Weight acts downwards and stays constant
Drag acts upwards and increases with speed
Resultant force = weight - drag
teach.note: Begin with a coin dropped in air: it feels weight and a very small drag. Ask pupils how drag would differ for a feather. Emphasise that weight does not change as the object falls, but drag does.
cycle: Start: speed zero, drag zero, resultant = weight
Speed rises, drag rises, acceleration falls
Drag becomes equal to weight
Resultant force zero: constant speed (terminal velocity)

teach.heading: Worked example: the skydiver
bullets: Mass 80 kg; use g = 10 N/kg
Find weight, resultant and acceleration when drag is 300 N
Find drag at terminal velocity
teach.note: Model aloud: always draw a free-body diagram first, label weight down and drag up. Note that at terminal velocity the object still moves; it just stops accelerating.

model.problem: An 80 kg skydiver falls. At one instant drag is 300 N. Calculate his acceleration. What is the drag at terminal velocity?
steps: At terminal velocity the resultant is zero, so drag = weight = 800 N
model.answer: a = 6.25 m/s² downwards; drag at terminal velocity = 800 N

teach.heading: The skydive on a velocity-time graph
bullets: Steep curve: large acceleration at the start
Curve flattens as drag grows
Horizontal line: terminal velocity
Parachute opens: speed drops, then a lower terminal velocity
teach.note: Sketch the graph live. Ask: what does the gradient show at each point? Why does opening the parachute make the resultant force point upwards for a moment? The numbers on the timeline are illustrative, not exact.

timeline.label: Chute opens
timeline.text: Drag greater than weight, slows down

teach.heading: Common errors
bullets: Heavier does not always mean faster in air
In a vacuum all objects fall with the same acceleration
Terminal velocity depends on shape and area as well as weight
teach.note: Mention the Apollo 15 hammer and feather demonstration on the Moon (1971). Contrast with a feather and coin in air. Link back: a = F/m, so a heavier object has more weight but also more mass.

misconception.wrong: At terminal velocity there are no forces acting on the object.
misconception.right: At terminal velocity two forces act, weight and drag, but they are equal and opposite, so the resultant force is zero.

teach.heading: Check: balanced forces
bullets: Choose the best statement
teach.note: Distractor A is the classic misconception that gravity stops. B has the forces the wrong way round. D confuses constant speed with no drag.

check.q: A parachutist falls at constant speed. Which statement is correct?
check.why: Constant speed means zero resultant force, so drag equals weight. Gravity always acts (A) and drag is not zero (D).

practice: A 0.050 kg ball bearing is dropped in oil. Weight is 0.50 N and drag is 0.20 N. Calculate the resultant force and acceleration.
Explain why a skydiver reaches a higher terminal velocity falling head-first than spread out.
A 70 kg parachutist falls at terminal velocity. State the drag force.
independent: Core: Describe in order the forces and motion of a skydiver from jumping to landing with a parachute.
Extend: Sketch a velocity-time graph for a parachutist who opens the parachute at 10 s. Label the terminal velocities and explain each section.
Stretch: Explain, using resultant force, why a raindrop falling from a high cloud does not hit the ground at very high speed.
exit: Define terminal velocity.
A 60 kg skydiver has drag 450 N. Calculate the acceleration (g = 10 N/kg).
lessons.homework: Design a parachute test using coffee filters: list the independent, dependent and control variables and one safety point.
lessons.send: SEND: provide the four-stage cycle as a card sort and a labelled free-body diagram. EAL: pre-teach drag, resistive, constant. Stretch: explain why terminal velocity depends on cross-sectional area.

lessons.title: Momentum and the conservation of momentum
lessons.bigQuestion: Why does a small bullet fired from a gun make the gun kick back?
objectives: Calculate momentum using p = mv
State and apply the conservation of momentum in collisions and explosions
successCriteria: All: calculate momentum
Most: use conservation of momentum for two objects sticking together
Some: solve explosion and recoil problems
lessons.crossCurricular: Maths: rearranging equations; PE: collisions in rugby
lessons.smsc: Moral: responsibility for the safe handling of equipment

keywords.def: mass multiplied by velocity, a vector measured in kg m/s
total momentum before = total momentum after, if no external force acts
two objects interacting briefly with large forces
objects pushed apart from rest

starter: Bismillah. A 1500 kg car moves at 20 m/s. Calculate its kinetic energy.
Which of these is a vector: speed, mass, velocity?
State Newton's first law.

teach.heading: Momentum
bullets: p = m × v
Unit: kg m/s
Vector: direction matters, so choose a positive direction
teach.note: Compare a lorry and a cyclist at the same speed. Pupils feel why the lorry is harder to stop. Emphasise that momentum has the direction of velocity, so +/- signs are essential.

model.problem: Calculate the momentum of a 1200 kg car moving at 15 m/s, and of a 0.15 kg cricket ball at 30 m/s.
steps: Same formula; unit is kg m/s
model.answer: Car 18 000 kg m/s; ball 4.5 kg m/s

teach.heading: Conservation of momentum
bullets: In a closed system, total momentum before = total momentum after
Applies to all collisions and explosions
Kinetic energy may not be conserved (inelastic collision)
teach.note: Use trolleys on a track with light gates if available. Method: 1) choose a positive direction, 2) write total p before, 3) write total p after, 4) equate. 'Closed' means no external forces such as friction.

model.problem: A 2.0 kg trolley moving at 3.0 m/s collides with a stationary 1.0 kg trolley. They stick together. Find their common velocity.
model.answer: Common velocity = 2.0 m/s in the original direction

teach.heading: Explosions and recoil
bullets: Before: at rest, so total momentum = 0
After: momenta equal in size and opposite in direction
The lighter object gets the higher speed
teach.note: Demonstrate with two spring-loaded trolleys pushed apart. Ask why the bullet gets a much greater speed than the gun: the momenta are equal and opposite, the bullet has far less mass, so its velocity is greater.

model.problem: A 4.0 kg rifle fires a 0.010 kg bullet at 400 m/s. Find the recoil velocity of the rifle.
steps: Rifle: 4.0 × v = -4.0 so that the total is 0
model.answer: Rifle recoils at 1.0 m/s opposite to the bullet

teach.heading: Check: collision
bullets: Use conservation of momentum
teach.note: Distractor A forgets the extra mass. C multiplies instead of conserving. Ask pupils to show their working on whiteboards.

check.q: A 3 kg trolley at 4 m/s hits and sticks to a stationary 1 kg trolley. What is the speed after?
check.why: Momentum before = 12 kg m/s. After: 4 kg × v = 12, so v = 3 m/s. A ignores the extra mass.

practice: Calculate the momentum of a 65 kg runner at 8.0 m/s.
A 0.50 kg trolley at 2.0 m/s hits a stationary 1.5 kg trolley and they stick together. Calculate their velocity.
A 60 kg skater at rest throws a 2 kg ball at 6 m/s. Calculate the skater's recoil velocity.
independent: Core: A 1000 kg car at 12 m/s hits a stationary 800 kg car and they lock together. Find the velocity after.
Extend: A 2 kg trolley moves right at 5 m/s and collides with a 3 kg trolley moving left at 2 m/s. They stick together. Find the velocity.
Stretch: A 0.20 kg ball at 6 m/s hits a 0.80 kg stationary ball, which moves off at 2.0 m/s. Find the velocity of the first ball and decide whether kinetic energy was conserved.
exit: State the principle of conservation of momentum.
A 5 kg cannon fires a 0.5 kg shell at 40 m/s. Calculate the cannon's recoil velocity.
lessons.homework: Write a half-page explanation of why a bullet gets a larger velocity than the gun, using the word 'momentum' at least four times.
lessons.send: SEND: provide a before/after momentum table for each object. EAL: sentence frames 'The momentum before is...'. Stretch: consider why kinetic energy is lost in sticking collisions.

lessons.title: Force as rate of change of momentum; Newton's third law
lessons.bigQuestion: How do crumple zones and airbags protect the people inside a car?
objectives: Use F = (mv - mu) ÷ t
Explain safety features in terms of change of momentum
State and apply Newton's third law
successCriteria: All: state Newton's third law
Most: calculate force from change in momentum and time
Some: explain safety features and identify third-law pairs correctly
lessons.crossCurricular: Engineering: vehicle safety; Maths: substitution and rearranging
lessons.smsc: Moral: protecting human life through careful design

keywords.def: change in momentum, equal to force × time
change in momentum divided by time taken, equal to force
when A pushes on B, B pushes on A with an equal and opposite force
part of a car designed to collapse and lengthen the collision time

starter: Bismillah. A 2 kg trolley at 3 m/s has what momentum?
A 5 kg object has a resultant force of 20 N. Find its acceleration.
State the unit of momentum.

teach.heading: Force as rate of change of momentum
bullets: Newton's second law: F = Δp ÷ t
F = (mv - mu) ÷ t
Longer time means smaller force for the same change in momentum
teach.note: Link to F = ma: substitute a = (v - u)/t into F = ma and show it matches. Pupils practise on whiteboards with simple numbers first.

model.problem: A 1200 kg car travelling at 20 m/s stops in 0.80 s in a crash. Calculate the average force on the car. Repeat for 2.0 s.
steps: F = Δp ÷ t = 24 000 ÷ 0.80 = 30 000 N (opposing the motion)

teach.heading: Safety features
bullets: Crumple zones, airbags and seat belts increase the stopping time
Same change in momentum, so smaller force
Smaller force means less injury
Gymnastics mats and cycle helmets work in the same way
teach.note: Ask pupils to explain crumple zones in a three-part sentence: increases time, reduces rate of change of momentum, so force is smaller. Use a raw egg dropped onto a pillow versus the floor as a thought experiment.

head: Feature
How it helps
rows: slows the head over a longer time and spreads the force
stretches slightly and stops the body with the car

teach.heading: Newton's third law
bullets: Forces always come in pairs between two objects
Equal in size, opposite in direction, same type of force
The pair act on different objects
teach.note: Use the example of a book on a table. The Earth pulling the book down pairs with the book pulling the Earth up, not with the contact force from the table. Ask pupils to name the pair for a rocket and for a swimmer pushing off the wall.

misconception.wrong: The two forces in a third-law pair cancel out, so nothing can ever move.
misconception.right: The forces act on different objects so they cannot cancel. A swimmer pushes the wall; the wall pushes the swimmer, who accelerates.

teach.heading: Check: crash force
bullets: Think about time and momentum
teach.note: A and D wrongly say momentum or mass changes. C is the opposite of the real effect.

check.q: A cyclist's helmet reduces injury because it...
options: increases the time taken to stop, reducing force
check.why: The change in momentum is fixed, so a longer stopping time gives a smaller force. The helmet does not change momentum or mass.

practice: A 0.057 kg tennis ball hits a racket at 40 m/s and leaves at 20 m/s in the opposite direction in 0.0050 s. Calculate the average force on the ball.
A 70 kg driver at 15 m/s is stopped by a seat belt in 0.30 s. Calculate the force.
Identify the third-law pair when a footballer kicks a ball.
independent: Core: Explain why a long jumper bends their knees on landing.
Extend: A 0.40 kg ball falls onto a floor at 6 m/s and rebounds at 4 m/s. Contact time is 0.020 s. Calculate the average force on the ball.
Stretch: A hose sprays 2.0 kg of water per second at 8 m/s on to a wall and stops it. Calculate the force on the wall.
exit: Show that a force of 24 N is needed to change the momentum of a trolley by 12 kg m/s in 0.50 s.
State the third-law partner of the Earth's pull on you.
lessons.homework: Write a short advert for a child car seat explaining, using momentum, why it is safer than a rigid seat.
lessons.send: SEND: sentence frame 'Same change in momentum, longer time, so smaller force'. EAL: pre-teach crumple, rebound. Stretch: derive F = Δp/t from F = ma.

lessons.title: Moments, centre of gravity and the principle of moments
lessons.bigQuestion: How can a small child balance an adult on a seesaw?
objectives: Calculate the moment of a force
Apply the principle of moments to a balanced object
Find the centre of gravity of a lamina and explain stability
successCriteria: All: calculate a moment
Most: use the principle of moments to find an unknown force or distance
Some: use a non-central pivot including the weight of a uniform beam
lessons.crossCurricular: Maths: rearranging equations; DT: levers and tools; PE: balance
lessons.smsc: Spiritual: balance and proportion in nature and in life

keywords.def: turning effect of a force: force × perpendicular distance from the pivot
the point about which an object turns
for balance, total clockwise moment = total anticlockwise moment
the point where the whole weight of an object seems to act

starter: Bismillah. Calculate the weight of a 40 kg child (g = 10 N/kg).
State the unit of force.
Explain what a resultant force of zero means for an object.

teach.heading: The moment of a force
bullets: Moment = force × perpendicular distance from the pivot
Unit: newton metre (N m)
A longer spanner gives a larger moment for the same force
teach.note: Demonstrate with a door: push near the hinge, then near the handle. Stress 'perpendicular' distance and convert cm to m before calculating.

model.problem: A mechanic pushes with 80 N on a spanner at 0.25 m from the nut. Find the moment. What force is needed at 0.40 m for the same moment?
steps: Same moment at 0.40 m: F = M ÷ d

teach.heading: The principle of moments
bullets: Balanced: clockwise moments = anticlockwise moments
The resultant moment is zero
Take moments about the pivot
teach.note: Practical: balance a metre rule on a pivot using 100 g masses; record the distances; check that W1 × d1 = W2 × d2 within experimental error. Independent variable: position of one mass; dependent: position of the other that balances. Safety: keep feet clear of falling masses.

model.problem: A child weighs 300 N and sits 2.0 m from the pivot of a seesaw. An adult weighs 600 N. Where must the adult sit to balance it?
model.answer: The adult sits 1.0 m from the pivot on the opposite side

teach.heading: Centre of gravity of a lamina
bullets: Centre of gravity: the point where the weight seems to act
Hang the lamina from a pin, with a plumb line
Mark the vertical line, repeat from two more holes
The lines cross at the centre of gravity
teach.note: Do the plumb-line practical in pairs. The lamina hangs freely so its centre of gravity ends directly below the pin. Safety: care with pins and loose plumb bobs. Three lines should cross at one point; a small triangle shows measurement error.
cycle: Make three holes near the edge of the card
Hang from hole 1 on a pin; hang a plumb line
Draw the vertical line along the string
Repeat with holes 2 and 3; lines cross at the centre of gravity

teach.heading: A beam with its own weight
bullets: A uniform beam's weight acts at its centre
Take moments about the pivot
Include the weight of the beam as a force
teach.note: Draw the ruler, label the pivot at 30 cm and the centre of gravity at 50 cm. Ask: which side does the beam's weight turn it? The upward force at the pivot has no moment about the pivot.

model.problem: A uniform metre rule weighs 1.2 N and is pivoted at the 30 cm mark. A weight hangs at the 5 cm mark to balance it. Find the weight.
steps: Rule's weight acts at 50 cm: distance from pivot = 20 cm = 0.20 m
Hung weight is at 25 cm = 0.25 m from the pivot

teach.heading: Stability
bullets: Stable: low centre of gravity and wide base
Tips when the weight line falls outside the base
Check: choose the correct reason
teach.note: Link to double-decker buses, which are tilt-tested, and racing cars. Ask pupils to tilt a box with a heavy base versus heavy top. Check using the options on the slide.

check.q: Why is a racing car with a low centre of gravity and wide wheelbase more stable?
options: The weight line stays inside the base until a larger tilt
check.why: The car can tilt further before the weight acts outside its base. Weight, momentum and drag are not the reason.

practice: A 25 N force acts 0.60 m from a pivot. Calculate the moment.
A 500 N boy sits 1.5 m from the pivot of a seesaw. Where must a 300 N girl sit to balance it?
Describe how to find the centre of gravity of an irregular piece of card.
independent: Core: A 40 N weight hangs 0.30 m left of a pivot. What force at 0.20 m on the right balances it?
Extend: A uniform 2.0 m plank weighs 80 N, pivoted at its centre. A 400 N person stands 0.50 m from one end. Where must a 600 N person stand to balance it?

Stretch: A 1.0 m uniform beam weighs 6.0 N and is pivoted at 0.20 m from one end. A 10 N weight hangs at the short end. Calculate the force needed 0.80 m from the pivot on the other side to keep it level, then the reaction force at the pivot.
exit: State the principle of moments.
A 50 N force acts 0.40 m from a pivot. Calculate the moment and give the unit.
lessons.homework: Write a method to find the centre of gravity of a lamina, listing the equipment and one safety precaution. Then complete four principle-of-moments problems.
lessons.send: SEND: give a labelled seesaw template: anticlockwise column and clockwise column. EAL: pre-teach pivot, clockwise, perpendicular. Stretch: include the pivot reaction force in the equilibrium of forces.

lessons.title: Mains electricity and safety: a.c., d.c., fuses and earthing
lessons.bigQuestion: How does a three-pin plug protect us when something goes wrong inside an appliance?
objectives: Compare a.c. and d.c.
Describe the live, neutral and earth wires of a plug
Explain how fuses, earthing, circuit breakers and insulation keep people safe
successCriteria: All: name the wires and their colours
Most: explain what a fuse and an earth wire do
Some: explain a fault sequence in a metal-cased appliance
lessons.crossCurricular: DT: product safety; Citizenship: electrical safety regulations
lessons.smsc: Moral: protecting life and property through care and responsibility

keywords.def: current that repeatedly reverses direction, as in UK mains (50 Hz)
current that flows in one direction only
a thin wire that melts if the current is too large, breaking the circuit
a safety wire that carries fault current safely to the ground

starter: Bismillah. State the SI unit of current and of potential difference.
Name the particles that carry current in a metal wire.
State the equation linking charge, current and time.

teach.heading: a.c. and d.c.
bullets: d.c.: flows one way (cells and batteries)
a.c.: reverses direction repeatedly
UK mains: about 230 V a.c., frequency 50 Hz
On an oscilloscope: d.c. is a flat line, a.c. is a wave
teach.note: Sketch both traces. Explain frequency 50 Hz means 50 complete reversals per second, so the period is 0.02 s. Ask pupils which type is used in their phone and which at the wall socket.

left.title: d.c.
points: Flat line on a voltage-time trace

teach.heading: Inside a three-pin plug
bullets: Live (brown): carries the supply voltage
Neutral (blue): completes the circuit
Earth (green and yellow): safety connection to the case
Fuse in the live wire
teach.note: Use a real plug or a labelled diagram. Ask why the fuse must be in the live wire: when it blows, the appliance is cut off from the 230 V. If it were in the neutral, the appliance would remain live. Switches also go in the live wire.

head: Part
Job
rows: melts when current is too high
stops the wires being pulled loose

teach.heading: What happens in a fault
bullets: A loose live wire touches the metal case
Case becomes live: a shock risk
Earth wire gives a low-resistance path to earth
Large current flows, fuse melts, appliance is isolated
teach.note: Walk through the steps slowly, and make clear that the earth wire only carries current when there is a fault. Mention circuit breakers (trip quickly, can be reset) and double-insulated appliances (plastic case, no earth wire needed).

model.problem: A toaster has a metal case. The live wire comes loose and touches the case. Explain how the earth wire and fuse protect the user.
steps: The earth wire connects the case to the ground
The live wire touching the case causes a large current through the earth wire
The large current heats and melts the fuse
The fuse breaks the live connection so the case is no longer live
model.answer: The fuse blows and isolates the toaster, so the case cannot give a shock

teach.heading: Danger zones
bullets: Damp conditions lower the body's resistance
Frayed cables expose live wires
Overloaded sockets can overheat
Wrong fuse rating is dangerous
teach.note: Stress practical safety: never use a plug with a damaged cable; never touch switches with wet hands; a fuse of too high a rating will not blow when it should. Discuss why protecting others from harm is part of good character.

misconception.wrong: The earth wire carries the current to make the appliance work.
misconception.right: The live and neutral wires carry the working current. The earth wire carries current only in a fault.

teach.heading: Check: where does the fuse go?
bullets: Select your answer
teach.note: Distractor B is a common error. Ask pupils to justify with a fault sequence.

check.q: In a three-pin plug the fuse is placed in the...
check.why: A fuse in the live wire disconnects the appliance from the 230 V supply when it blows. In the neutral wire, the appliance would stay connected to the live supply.

practice: State two differences between a.c. and d.c.
A plastic-cased hairdryer has no earth wire. Explain why it is still safe.
Explain why a fuse is placed in the live wire and not the neutral wire.
independent: Core: Label a diagram of a three-pin plug with wire colours and the fuse.
Extend: Explain why a person with wet hands is at greater risk of an electric shock.
Stretch: An a.c. supply has a period of 0.020 s. Calculate its frequency and say what happens to the direction of the current in 0.020 s.
exit: Name the three wires in a UK plug and their colours.
Explain what happens to an earthed metal appliance if the live wire touches the case.
lessons.homework: Make an electrical-safety poster for the home that includes three hazards and how a fuse, earth or circuit breaker protects against them.
lessons.send: SEND: colour-coded wire matching card and plug diagram. EAL: pre-teach live, neutral, fuse, earth. Stretch: explain residual current devices that compare live and neutral currents.

lessons.title: Electrical power and energy: P = IV, E = IVt and choosing fuses
lessons.bigQuestion: How do we know which fuse to put in the plug of a kettle?
objectives: Calculate electrical power using P = IV
Calculate energy transferred using E = IVt
Choose a suitable fuse
successCriteria: All: use P = IV
Most: use E = IVt, converting minutes to seconds
Some: choose a fuse and explain the choice
lessons.crossCurricular: Maths: rearranging; Economics: cost of electricity
lessons.smsc: Moral: avoiding waste (israf) in the use of energy

keywords.def: rate of energy transfer, measured in watts (W)
one joule of energy transferred per second
the current at which the fuse is designed to melt
1000 watts

starter: Bismillah. Calculate the voltage across a 4 Ω resistor carrying 3 A.
Convert 5 minutes to seconds.
Explain what a fuse does.

teach.heading: Electrical power
bullets: Power = current × potential difference
P = I × V
Watts = amps × volts
teach.note: Link to prior knowledge: power is the energy per second. A 2.3 kW kettle transfers 2300 J each second. Show the rating labels on appliances. Pupils should write unit symbols in every line of working.

model.problem: A kettle works from the 230 V mains and draws a current of 10 A. Calculate its power.

teach.heading: Energy transferred
bullets: E = I × V × t
Also E = P × t
Time must be in seconds
Energy in joules
teach.note: Derive: energy = power × time, and power = IV. Common error: using minutes. Do one example with a calculator-free number first.

model.problem: A 12 V motor draws 3.0 A for 5.0 minutes. Calculate the energy transferred.

teach.heading: Choosing a fuse
bullets: Calculate the normal current: I = P ÷ V
Choose the next fuse rating above it
Common ratings: 3 A, 5 A, 13 A
teach.note: Ask: why not use the nearest rating below? It would blow every time. Why not 13 A for everything? A fault current of 8 A in a 5 A appliance would not blow a 13 A fuse and the wire could overheat.

model.problem: A 920 W toaster uses the 230 V mains. Which fuse should be fitted: 3 A, 5 A or 13 A?
steps: Fuse must be just above 4.0 A

teach.heading: Cost of electricity (extension)
bullets: kilowatt-hour (kWh) = 1 kW for 1 hour
Energy (kWh) = power (kW) × time (h)
Cost = energy in kWh × price per kWh
teach.note: Show a bill excerpt. Example: a 2 kW heater for 3 h uses 6 kWh; at 30p/kWh that costs £1.80. Link to avoiding waste when a device is not needed.

misconception.wrong: A 13 A fuse is the safest for every appliance.
misconception.right: The fuse should have a rating just above the normal current. Too large a rating will not melt in a fault, so the wire may overheat.

teach.heading: Check: fuse choice
bullets: Calculate, then choose
teach.note: The normal current is 1000 ÷ 230 = 4.3 A. A is the nearest below, so it would blow in normal use. C and D are too high.

check.q: A 1000 W appliance runs from 230 V mains. Which fuse is best?
check.why: I = 1000 ÷ 230 = 4.3 A. A 3 A fuse would blow in normal use; 13 A or 30 A are too high for protection.

practice: Calculate the power of a lamp using 0.26 A at 230 V.
A 6.0 V bulb transfers 36 J in 6.0 s. Calculate the power and the current.
A 3.0 kW heater works at 230 V. Calculate the current and choose from 3 A, 5 A and 13 A fuses.
independent: Core: A hairdryer is rated 1800 W at 230 V. Calculate the current and recommend a fuse.
Extend: A 230 V, 2.0 A drill runs for 15 minutes. Calculate the energy transferred in joules and in kWh.
Stretch: A 2.4 kW immersion heater runs for 25 minutes. The cost is 28p per kWh. Calculate the cost to the nearest penny.
exit: Write the equation linking energy, current, potential difference and time.
A 1.5 kW heater is on for 2 hours. How many kWh does it use?
lessons.homework: Find the power rating of five appliances at home, calculate each current at 230 V and say which fuse would be suitable.
lessons.send: SEND: use a three-step template: write the formula, substitute, answer with unit. EAL: pre-teach rating, fuse, kWh. Stretch: explain why power cables are rated by current.

lessons.title: Series and parallel circuits: current, voltage, resistance and charge
lessons.bigQuestion: Why do Christmas lights in an old string go out together, but the lights in a house do not?
objectives: Describe current and voltage rules in series and parallel circuits
Use V = IR and Q = It
Explain why current is conserved at junctions
successCriteria: All: state the series and parallel rules
Most: calculate current and voltage using V = IR
Some: solve combined series and parallel problems
lessons.crossCurricular: Maths: rearranging; DT: circuit design
lessons.smsc: Spiritual: order and design in systems we rely on

keywords.def: energy transferred per unit charge, measured in volts
opposition to current, measured in ohms (Ω)
components in a single loop
components on separate branches

starter: Bismillah. State the equation for electrical power.
Name the instrument that measures current and say how it is connected.
State what the unit of resistance is.

teach.heading: Series circuits
bullets: One loop: same current everywhere
Supply voltage is shared across components
Total resistance = R₁ + R₂
If one component fails, all stop
teach.note: Build a series circuit from cells and bulbs. Pupils predict ammeter readings in different places. Voltmeters go in parallel with the component, ammeters in series.

model.problem: A 12 V supply is connected to a 4 Ω and an 8 Ω resistor in series. Find the current and the voltage across each resistor.

teach.heading: Parallel circuits
bullets: Branches: voltage across each branch equals the supply
Current splits at a junction and recombines
Current into a junction = current out
Each branch works independently
teach.note: Draw the junction as a river splitting. Ask: where has the current gone? (Nowhere: charge is conserved.) The branch with lower resistance carries more current. This is why household sockets are in parallel.

model.problem: A 6.0 V supply is connected to a 12 Ω and a 6.0 Ω resistor in parallel. Find the current in each branch and the total current.

teach.heading: Charge, current and time
bullets: Q = I × t
Charge in coulombs (C)
Current is rate of flow of charge: 1 A = 1 C per second
teach.note: Link back to the ammeter reading: an ammeter measures how much charge passes each second. Ask: how much charge passes a point at 2.5 A for 40 s?

model.problem: A current of 2.5 A flows through a lamp for 40 s. Calculate the charge that flows.

teach.heading: Series versus parallel
bullets: Series: same current, voltages add
Parallel: same voltage, currents add
Check: use the right rule
teach.note: Use the check as a hinge. Ask for reasons; the common error is mixing current and voltage rules.

check.q: Two identical bulbs are in parallel across a 6 V cell. What is the voltage across each bulb?
check.why: Each parallel branch has the full supply voltage of 6 V. 3 V would be the share in series.

practice: Calculate the current through a 15 Ω resistor connected to a 3.0 V cell.
Three resistors of 2 Ω, 3 Ω and 5 Ω are in series with a 20 V supply. Calculate the current and the voltage across the 5 Ω resistor.
A current of 0.80 A flows for 2.0 minutes. Calculate the charge.
independent: Core: In a series circuit the ammeter reads 0.40 A and a voltmeter across one resistor reads 2.0 V. Calculate its resistance.
Extend: A 12 V battery supplies two parallel branches of 24 Ω and 8.0 Ω. Calculate the current from the battery.
Stretch: A 12 V supply is connected to a 6 Ω resistor in series with two 12 Ω resistors in parallel. Calculate the total current from the supply. (Parallel pair: 1/R = 1/12 + 1/12.)
exit: State the rule for current at a junction.
Calculate the charge when 3.0 A flows for 20 s.
lessons.homework: Draw one series and one parallel circuit with a cell, two lamps, an ammeter and a voltmeter. Label the readings you would predict for 6 V and lamps of equal resistance.
lessons.send: SEND: coloured series and parallel summary card with rules; EAL: key terms in L1 and L2 glossary. Stretch: derive the parallel resistance formula.

lessons.title: Current-voltage characteristics: resistors, lamps, diodes, LDRs and thermistors
lessons.bigQuestion: Why does a lamp's resistance change when it is switched on, but a fixed resistor's does not?
objectives: Describe the I-V graphs for a resistor, filament lamp and diode
Describe how an LDR and a thermistor behave
Plan an investigation to find I-V characteristics
successCriteria: All: recognise the I-V graph shapes
Most: explain each shape and calculate resistance at a point
Some: plan a safe investigation and evaluate results
lessons.crossCurricular: Maths: gradients and graphs; Computing: sensors
lessons.smsc: Moral: honest recording and reporting of results

keywords.def: a conductor whose resistance stays constant, so I is proportional to V
a component that conducts in one direction only
light-dependent resistor: resistance falls as light intensity rises
resistor whose resistance falls as temperature rises (NTC)

starter: Bismillah. Calculate the resistance when 6.0 V gives a current of 0.30 A.
Explain why a voltmeter is connected in parallel.
Sketch a straight line through the origin and state what it shows.

teach.heading: Core practical: investigating I-V
bullets: Series circuit with component, ammeter, variable resistor
Voltmeter in parallel across the component
Change the voltage in steps; record V and I
Repeat with reversed battery for a diode
teach.note: Pupils set up circuits in pairs. Independent variable: potential difference; dependent: current; controls: temperature (keep currents small for the resistor), same component. Safety: lamp and resistor can get hot; do not exceed the rated voltage. Take repeat readings and plot I (y-axis) against V (x-axis).
cycle: Set up the circuit with the component, ammeter and variable resistor
Place the voltmeter across the component
Adjust the variable resistor to get a set of V and I readings
Reverse the cell connections and repeat
Plot I against V and draw a smooth line

teach.heading: The graphs
bullets: Resistor at constant temperature: straight line through the origin
Filament lamp: curve flattens as V rises
Diode: no current in reverse; conducts above about 0.6 V forward
Resistance = V ÷ I at each point
teach.note: Sketch each on the board. The lamp filament heats up; ions vibrate more, collisions with electrons increase, so resistance increases. The gradient of an I-V graph is 1/R, so a shallower gradient means higher resistance.

head: Component
I-V shape
Reason
rows: resistance rises as the filament heats
zero current in reverse, steep rise forward

teach.heading: Worked example: resistance of a lamp
bullets: Resistance is V ÷ I at that point
Not the gradient of the curve
Resistance changes along the curve
teach.note: Use data from a practical. Pupils often treat the gradient as the resistance; the correct statement is that R = V/I at each point.

model.problem: A filament lamp has a current of 0.40 A at 2.0 V and 1.5 A at 12 V. Calculate the resistance at each point and explain the change.
steps: The higher current heats the filament
Hotter filament: more collisions, so higher resistance
model.answer: 5.0 Ω at 2.0 V and 8.0 Ω at 12 V; resistance rises as the filament gets hotter

teach.heading: LDRs and thermistors
bullets: LDR: resistance falls as light gets brighter
Thermistor: resistance falls as temperature rises
Uses: automatic lights, fire alarms, thermostats
teach.note: Link to a street-light circuit: dark means high LDR resistance. Practical idea: use a lamp at different distances from an LDR and measure resistance. Many thermistors in GCSE questions are NTC types.

misconception.wrong: Resistance of every component is constant, so I-V graphs are always straight lines.
misconception.right: Only an ohmic conductor at constant temperature has a straight line. Lamps, diodes, LDRs and thermistors have changing resistance.

teach.heading: Check: diode
bullets: Pick the correct statement
teach.note: Option A confuses a diode with a resistor. D describes the lamp.

check.q: A diode is connected in reverse. The current is...
check.why: A diode has a very high resistance in the reverse direction, so almost no current flows.

practice: Calculate the resistance of a resistor that carries 0.25 A when the p.d. across it is 5.0 V.
Explain the shape of the I-V graph for a filament lamp.
A thermistor has a resistance of 2000 Ω at 20°C. State what happens to its resistance when warmed.
independent: Core: Describe how you would obtain data to plot an I-V graph for a resistor, including the circuit symbols to use.
Extend: Sketch the I-V graph for a diode and explain why current only flows in one direction (forward bias).
Stretch: An LDR is in a circuit. Its resistance is 800 Ω in bright light and 40 000 Ω in the dark, at 6 V. Calculate the current in each case and explain how this could switch on a street lamp.
exit: Which component has an I-V graph that is a straight line through the origin?
State what happens to the resistance of an LDR when light intensity increases.
lessons.homework: Draw labelled I-V sketches for a resistor, filament lamp and diode and write one sentence under each to explain its shape.
lessons.send: SEND: give pre-drawn axes and sketches to match to components. EAL: key terms in pairs (ohmic, filament, diode). Stretch: use thermistor and resistor as a potential divider.

lessons.title: Potential difference, charge and the flow of electrons
lessons.bigQuestion: What actually moves in a wire when we switch on a light?
objectives: Define potential difference as energy transferred per unit charge
Use E = QV
Explain current as a flow of electrons and distinguish it from conventional current
successCriteria: All: describe current as flow of charge
Most: calculate charge and energy using Q = It and E = QV
Some: explain why current is the same everywhere in a series circuit
lessons.crossCurricular: Chemistry: metallic bonding; Maths: standard form
lessons.smsc: Spiritual: wonder at unseen particles which explain everyday things

keywords.def: a property of matter measured in coulombs (C)
negatively charged particle that carries current in metals
direction of flow from positive to negative terminal
energy transferred per coulomb of charge, E = QV

starter: Bismillah. Calculate the charge passing when 2.0 A flows for 30 s.
State the charge on an electron: positive or negative?
Calculate the power of a 12 V, 3 A motor.

teach.heading: Current is flow of charge
bullets: Metals contain free (delocalised) electrons
The cell makes the electrons drift through the wire
Current = rate of flow of charge: Q = I × t
Electrons are not used up
teach.note: Show the wire as a lattice of positive ions with a sea of electrons. The electrons drift slowly but a push travels fast, like a full pipe of water. Ask: if the electrons were used up in the bulb, how would the current at the far end differ? (It would be smaller; it is not.)

left.title: Conventional current
points: Used for the left-hand rule later

teach.heading: Potential difference
bullets: Potential difference is energy transferred per unit charge
E = Q × V
1 volt = 1 joule per coulomb
A 12 V battery gives 12 J to each coulomb
teach.note: Treat potential difference as a measure of the 'push' each coulomb gets from a cell and the energy each coulomb loses in a component. Avoid the word 'voltage used up': the energy is transferred, the charge continues.

model.problem: A current of 3.0 A flows for 20 s through a 12 V motor. Calculate the charge and the energy transferred.

teach.heading: Same current everywhere in series
bullets: Charge cannot disappear
What flows into a bulb flows out
Same ammeter reading either side of a lamp
teach.note: Pupils often think the bulb uses up the current. Use a water-wheel analogy: the water arrives and leaves at the same rate, but loses energy on the way.

misconception.wrong: A bulb uses up the current, so the ammeter after it reads less.
misconception.right: The current is the same before and after the bulb. The bulb transfers energy from each coulomb, so the potential difference falls but the charge keeps flowing.

teach.heading: Check: energy per coulomb
bullets: Choose one answer
teach.note: Distractor A is the definition of current. C and D mix up quantities.

check.q: A 9.0 V battery transfers 54 J of energy. How much charge has passed?
check.why: Q = E ÷ V = 54 ÷ 9.0 = 6.0 C. 486 comes from multiplying instead of dividing.

practice: A lamp passes 0.50 A for 2.0 minutes. Calculate the charge that flows.
How much energy is transferred when 40 C of charge passes through a potential difference of 6.0 V?
A battery transfers 360 J to 30 C of charge. Calculate its potential difference.
independent: Core: Explain the difference between conventional current and electron flow.
Extend: A kettle element passes 10 A for 3.0 minutes at 230 V. Calculate the charge and the energy transferred.
Stretch: The charge on one electron is 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C. Calculate how many electrons pass a point when a current of 0.80 A flows for 10 s.
exit: Define potential difference using the words energy and charge.
State why the ammeter reading is the same on both sides of a lamp in a series circuit.
lessons.homework: Write a 100-word explanation for a younger pupil of what moves in a wire and what the battery does, avoiding the phrase 'used up'.
lessons.send: SEND: bar-model diagram for E = QV. EAL: pre-teach drift, delocalised, conventional. Stretch: derive E = IVt from Q = It and E = QV.

lessons.title: Static electricity: charging by friction, uses and dangers
lessons.bigQuestion: Why can a balloon rubbed on a jumper stick to a wall?
objectives: Explain charging by friction using electron transfer
Describe attraction and repulsion between charges
Describe uses and dangers of static electricity
successCriteria: All: state that like charges repel and unlike attract
Most: explain how an insulator becomes charged by rubbing
Some: explain an application or danger of static in detail, including earthing
lessons.crossCurricular: Chemistry: atoms and electrons; Geography: lightning
lessons.smsc: Spiritual: awe at natural forces such as lightning, and humility before them

keywords.def: charge that builds up on an insulator and stays there
rubbing, which can transfer electrons between surfaces
a material that does not let charge flow through it
connecting a charged object to the ground so charge flows away

starter: Bismillah. State the charge on a proton, neutron and electron.
Which particles move when current flows in a metal wire?
Give one use of an insulator.

teach.heading: Charging by friction
bullets: Rubbing transfers electrons from one insulator to another
The surface that gains electrons becomes negative
The surface that loses electrons becomes positive
Only electrons move, never protons
teach.note: Demonstrate with a polythene rod and cloth, using a hanging charged rod and a paper strip. Ask which gains electrons for polythene rubbed with a cloth: the rod gains electrons (negative), the cloth loses them (positive). Both end up with equal and opposite charges.

model.problem: A polythene rod is rubbed with a dry cloth. The rod becomes negatively charged. Explain how.
steps: Both begin with equal positive and negative charges
Friction transfers electrons from the cloth to the rod
The rod has gained extra electrons so has a negative charge
The cloth has lost electrons so is positively charged
model.answer: Electrons move from the cloth to the rod; the rod is negative and the cloth positive

teach.heading: Forces between charges
bullets: Like charges repel
Unlike charges attract
A charged insulator attracts small neutral objects
The force is greater when the charges are closer
teach.note: Show two hanging charged rods repelling and a rod with a cloth attracting. Explain how a charged object attracts neutral paper: charges in the paper redistribute, so the near side has opposite charge and is attracted.

check.q: Two negatively charged balloons are brought close together. What happens?
check.why: Like charges repel. Option A is unlike charges; C and D are not correct because both carry negative charge.

teach.heading: Uses of static
bullets: Electrostatic spraying: paint droplets repel and coat evenly
Electrostatic precipitators remove smoke particles in chimneys
Photocopiers and laser printers use charged drums
teach.note: Explain the spray gun: the droplets all gain the same charge so repel and spread evenly; the object is oppositely charged or earthed so attracts the paint, wrapping around the back. This is a typical exam scenario.

head: Use
How it works
rows: droplets charged by the gun repel; attracted to earthed object
charged plates attract charged smoke particles
charged drum attracts oppositely charged toner

teach.heading: Dangers and earthing
bullets: Sparks can ignite fuel vapour or flammable gases
Lightning is a large discharge
Aircraft and tankers are earthed when refuelling
Earthing lets charge flow safely to the ground
teach.note: Explain how a fuel tanker is earthed to stop a spark. Also clothes crackling and small shocks from car doors. Remind pupils that the safest response to lightning is to shelter, not stand under tall trees, which is common-sense safety.

misconception.wrong: Charging by friction creates new charge from nothing.
misconception.right: Charge is not created. Electrons are transferred from one object to another, so total charge stays the same.

practice: Describe how a balloon becomes charged when rubbed on hair.
Explain why car refuelling hoses are earthed.
A positively charged rod is brought near a hanging negatively charged ball. State what happens and why.
independent: Core: Explain how an electrostatic precipitator removes smoke particles.
Extend: A rod charged negatively touches an uncharged metal sphere on an insulating stand. Describe what happens to the electrons and the final charge on the sphere.
Stretch: Explain, in terms of charge movement, why a charged plastic comb picks up small pieces of neutral paper.
exit: State which particle is transferred when an insulator is charged by friction.
Give one use and one danger of static electricity.
lessons.homework: Research one real application of static electricity and write a paragraph explaining how charge makes it work.
lessons.send: SEND: step cards for electron transfer with drawings. EAL: pre-teach attract, repel, discharge. Stretch: explain charging by induction using an earthed sphere.

lessons.title: Wave basics: types of wave, v = fλ and f = 1/T
lessons.bigQuestion: What is the same, and what is different, about a ripple on a pond and a sound from a speaker?
objectives: Describe transverse and longitudinal waves
Define amplitude, wavelength, frequency and period
Use v = fλ and f = 1/T
successCriteria: All: label amplitude and wavelength on a wave
Most: calculate wave speed, frequency or period
Some: rearrange and use both equations in multi-step problems
lessons.crossCurricular: Maths: rearranging, standard form; Music: pitch and frequency
lessons.smsc: Spiritual: wonder at the patterns found in nature

keywords.def: the distance between two matching points on neighbouring waves (m)
the number of complete waves passing a point each second (Hz)
maximum displacement from the rest position
the time for one complete wave, T = 1 ÷ f

starter: Bismillah. Rearrange v = d ÷ t to make t the subject.
Convert 2.5 kHz to Hz.
Convert 0.040 s to milliseconds.

teach.heading: Two kinds of wave
bullets: Transverse: vibrations at right angles to the direction of travel
Longitudinal: vibrations parallel to the direction of travel
Longitudinal waves have compressions and rarefactions
teach.note: Demonstrate with a slinky: push-pull for longitudinal, side-to-side for transverse. Examples: water, light and all EM waves are transverse; sound and pressure waves in a spring are longitudinal.

left.title: Transverse
points: Vibration at 90° to the wave direction
e.g. light, water ripples, EM waves

teach.heading: Describing a wave
bullets: Amplitude: maximum displacement from the middle
Wavelength λ: peak to peak (m)
Frequency f: waves per second (Hz)
Period T: time for one wave (s)
teach.note: Draw a displacement-distance graph and label. Emphasise that amplitude is measured from the rest line, not peak to trough. The period uses a displacement-time graph.

model.problem: A wave has a frequency of 50 Hz and a wavelength of 0.20 m. Calculate its speed and its period.

teach.heading: Core practical idea: speed of water waves
bullets: Ripple tank with a vibrating dipper at a known frequency
Freeze the pattern with a strobe or a camera
Measure the wavelength over several waves, then divide
Calculate v = fλ
teach.note: Method: measure the distance across 10 wavelengths and divide by 10 to reduce error. Independent variable: frequency of the dipper; dependent: wavelength; controls: depth of water. Expected result: higher frequency, shorter wavelength; speed stays constant in the same depth. Safety: keep mains equipment away from water spills.

model.problem: In a ripple tank, 8 wavelengths span 0.24 m. The dipper vibrates at 5.0 Hz. Find the wave speed.

teach.heading: Check: rearranging
bullets: Choose the correct answer
teach.note: Option A is a division error; C has multiplied instead of dividing. Ask for the rearranged equation first.

check.q: Sound travels at 340 m/s. A note has a wavelength of 0.68 m. What is its frequency?
check.why: f = v ÷ λ = 340 ÷ 0.68 = 500 Hz. 231 comes from 340 × 0.68; 0.002 inverts the equation.

practice: A wave has a frequency of 2.0 Hz and a wavelength of 1.5 m. Calculate the speed.
A wave has a period of 0.040 s. Calculate its frequency.
Light travels at 3.0 × 10⁸ m/s. Calculate the wavelength of light of frequency 6.0 × 10¹⁴ Hz.
independent: Core: Describe the difference between a transverse and a longitudinal wave, with one example of each.
Extend: A wave on a rope travels at 4.0 m/s with a wavelength of 0.50 m. Calculate the frequency and the period.
Stretch: Waves on a lake travel at 2.4 m/s. A boat meets a wave crest every 1.5 s. Calculate the wavelength and explain what changes if the boat moves towards the waves.
exit: State the equation linking wave speed, frequency and wavelength.
A wave has a frequency of 25 Hz. State its period.
lessons.homework: Draw a transverse wave and label amplitude and wavelength. Then complete four wave-speed calculations including one that needs standard form.
lessons.send: SEND: give labelled wave templates and a triangle for v = fλ. EAL: pre-teach crest, trough, compression. Stretch: explain why the wave speed remains constant when frequency changes.

lessons.title: Wave properties: energy transfer, reflection, refraction and the Doppler effect
lessons.bigQuestion: Why does an ambulance siren seem to change pitch as it passes you?
objectives: Explain that waves transfer energy without transferring matter
Describe reflection and refraction of waves using wavefronts
Describe the Doppler effect
successCriteria: All: state that waves transfer energy, not matter
Most: describe what happens to speed, wavelength and frequency in refraction
Some: explain the Doppler effect in terms of wavefronts
lessons.crossCurricular: Geography: tsunamis; Music: the pitch of sirens
lessons.smsc: Spiritual: wonder at the unseen energy travelling through the world

keywords.def: a wave bouncing off a surface
a change in direction when a wave changes speed entering a different medium
a line joining points of the same phase of a wave
the change in observed frequency when source and observer move relative to each other

starter: Bismillah. Calculate the speed of a wave with f = 12 Hz and λ = 0.50 m.
Is sound transverse or longitudinal?
State the unit of frequency.

teach.heading: Energy, not matter
bullets: A wave moves energy from place to place
The particles of the medium only vibrate about their position
A floating cork bobs up and down but is not carried along
teach.note: Place a cork in a ripple tank. Ask what travels and what stays. Link to tsunami energy and a Mexican wave crowd. Ask: how can sound waves move across a room if the air only vibrates?

misconception.wrong: Water waves carry the water along with them to the shore.
misconception.right: Waves transfer energy. The water mostly moves in small circles or up and down; the wave pattern travels, not the water itself.

teach.heading: Reflection and refraction of waves
bullets: Reflection: angle of incidence = angle of reflection
Refraction: wave changes speed when it enters a new medium
Frequency stays the same; speed and wavelength change
Slower medium: shorter wavelength and bends towards the normal
teach.note: Use a ripple tank with a glass plate to create a shallow region. Ask why the wavefronts bend: the part entering the shallow region first slows first. The frequency is set by the source and cannot change at the boundary.

model.problem: Water waves of frequency 5.0 Hz travel at 0.20 m/s in deep water. They enter shallow water with wavelength 0.024 m. Find the wavelength in deep water and the speed in shallow water.
model.answer: Deep λ = 0.040 m; shallow speed = 0.12 m/s

teach.heading: The Doppler effect
bullets: Source moving towards you: waves squashed, higher frequency
Source moving away: waves stretched, lower frequency
Speed of the wave in the medium does not change
teach.note: Draw circular wavefronts from a moving source: bunched ahead and spread behind. Use an ambulance siren or a speeding car. Link to red-shift of light from distant galaxies in Physics 8.

timeline.label: Approaching
timeline.text: Wavefronts bunched, short wavelength, high pitch

timeline.label: Receding
timeline.text: Wavefronts stretched, long wavelength, low pitch

teach.heading: Check: refraction
bullets: Pick the correct statement
teach.note: Option B is the common mistake; frequency is set by the source. A and D confuse speed with direction.

check.q: A wave slows down when it enters a new medium. Which quantity stays the same?
check.why: Frequency depends on the source, so it stays the same. Speed and wavelength decrease; direction may change.

practice: Explain why a cork bobs up and down but does not move across a pond as waves pass.
A police car siren sounds higher as it approaches than as it moves away. Explain this.
Waves in a ripple tank slow down when they enter a shallow region. State what happens to wavelength and frequency.
independent: Core: Draw wavefronts bending when they enter a shallow region.
Extend: Waves of frequency 4.0 Hz have wavelength 0.050 m in deep water and 0.030 m in shallow water. Calculate the speed in each region.
Stretch: Explain why the Doppler effect for a moving source changes wavelength but not wave speed, using wavefront diagrams.
exit: State what a wave transfers.
State what happens to the pitch of a source as it moves away from you.
lessons.homework: Draw two diagrams of wavefronts from a moving source and annotate how an observer hears the pitch change.
lessons.send: SEND: provide printed wavefront diagrams to annotate. EAL: pre-teach reflect, refract, observer. Stretch: use the relative-speed approach to compute frequencies.

lessons.title: The electromagnetic spectrum: uses and hazards
lessons.bigQuestion: Why can radio waves pass through a wall and X-rays pass through a hand, but light cannot?
objectives: Order the regions of the electromagnetic spectrum
State that all EM waves travel at the same speed in a vacuum
Describe uses and hazards of each region
successCriteria: All: order the EM spectrum
Most: give a use and a hazard for each region
Some: calculate wavelength or frequency using c = fλ and justify a use
lessons.crossCurricular: Biology: UV and skin cancer; Technology: communications
lessons.smsc: Moral: using technology wisely, with consideration of safety

keywords.def: a transverse wave that can travel through a vacuum at 3.0 × 10⁸ m/s
radiation that can remove electrons from atoms, damaging cells
heat radiation, between visible light and microwaves
very high-frequency EM radiation from the nucleus

starter: Bismillah. Calculate the frequency of a wave with speed 340 m/s and wavelength 0.34 m.
State whether light is longitudinal or transverse.
Name two colours of the visible spectrum.

teach.heading: The spectrum in order
bullets: Radio, microwave, infrared, visible, ultraviolet, X-ray, gamma
From left to right: frequency and energy increase
Wavelength decreases
All are transverse and travel at 3.0 × 10⁸ m/s in a vacuum
teach.note: Give a mnemonic and let pupils create their own. Draw an arrow showing the direction of increasing frequency. Within visible light: red has the longest wavelength, violet the shortest.

teach.heading: Uses and hazards
bullets: Match each wave to its property
Higher-frequency waves carry more energy
UV, X-rays and gamma can damage cells
teach.note: Pupils fill in the table from memory first, then correct. The hazard is linked to energy: microwaves heat tissue; infrared causes burns; UV causes sunburn, eye damage and skin cancer; X-rays and gamma ionise cells, causing mutation and cancer.

teach.heading: Using c = fλ
bullets: All EM waves: c = 3.0 × 10⁸ m/s in a vacuum
c = f × λ
Short wavelength means high frequency
teach.note: Remind pupils of standard form on the calculator (EXP key). Typical radio-frequency questions use MHz; convert to Hz first (1 MHz = 10⁶ Hz).

model.problem: A radio station broadcasts with wavelength 3.0 m. Calculate the frequency. (c = 3.0 × 10⁸ m/s)

teach.heading: Check: hazard and energy
bullets: Choose one
teach.note: Option A is the common misconception that microwave ovens make food radioactive. Ask for the link between frequency and energy.

check.q: Which wave has the highest frequency and can damage living cells by ionisation?
check.why: Gamma rays have the highest frequency and energy in the spectrum, and they ionise atoms. Microwaves and infrared mainly heat tissue.

practice: List the seven regions of the EM spectrum in order of increasing frequency.
Calculate the wavelength of an EM wave of frequency 5.0 × 10¹⁴ Hz.
Explain why UV radiation is harmful to skin but radio waves are not.
independent: Core: Match uses to waves: sterilising food, TV remote control, mobile phone signals, security marking.
Extend: A mobile phone signal has frequency 900 MHz. Calculate its wavelength in m.
Stretch: A radiographer wears a lead apron and stands behind a screen. Explain, using properties of X-rays, why these precautions are needed and why the patient accepts the risk.
exit: State the speed of all EM waves in a vacuum.
State one hazard of ultraviolet radiation.
lessons.homework: Create a one-page fact file for one region of the EM spectrum covering a use, a hazard, a precaution and an example calculation using c = fλ.
lessons.send: SEND: provide a labelled spectrum strip with arrows for frequency and wavelength. EAL: pre-teach ionise, sterilise. Stretch: justify risk-benefit for X-ray imaging.

lessons.title: Reflection and refraction of light: ray diagrams and refractive index
lessons.bigQuestion: Why does a straw look broken in a glass of water?
objectives: State and use the law of reflection
Draw ray diagrams for reflection in a plane mirror and refraction in glass
Calculate refractive index using n = sin i ÷ sin r
successCriteria: All: use the law of reflection and describe the image in a plane mirror
Most: describe refraction and draw rays correctly
Some: calculate n and the angle of refraction and plan the glass-block practical
lessons.crossCurricular: Maths: trigonometry; Art: perspective and reflections
lessons.smsc: Spiritual: appreciating the scholars of the Islamic Golden Age; Ibn al-Haytham (about 965-1040) wrote the Book of Optics and used experiments to study light

keywords.def: a line at 90° to the surface where a ray meets it
angle between the incident ray and the normal
n = sin i ÷ sin r, a measure of how much a material bends light
an image that cannot be projected onto a screen

starter: Bismillah. State the speed of light in a vacuum.
Name two other EM waves besides light.
Calculate sin 30° using your calculator.

teach.heading: Reflection
bullets: Angles are measured from the normal
Angle of incidence = angle of reflection
Plane mirror image: virtual, same size, same distance behind the mirror
Left and right appear swapped
teach.note: Use ray boxes and plane mirrors. Insist on dashed lines for virtual rays and arrows on real rays. Ask: where is the image if you stand 2 m from the mirror? (2 m behind it, so 4 m from you.)

check.q: A ray hits a plane mirror at 35° to the normal. What is the angle between the incident and reflected rays?
check.why: Angle of incidence = angle of reflection = 35°, so the angle between the rays is 70°. 55° is the angle to the mirror surface.

teach.heading: Refraction in glass
bullets: Light changes speed at a boundary and bends
Into a denser medium: bends towards the normal
Out of a denser medium: bends away from the normal
No bending if the ray is along the normal
teach.note: Show a ray passing through a rectangular glass block: the emerging ray is parallel to the incident ray but shifted sideways. Explain the straw: light from the straw bends at the water surface and the brain traces it back in a straight line.
cycle: Ray enters glass: slows and bends towards the normal
Ray travels straight through the glass
Ray leaves glass: speeds up and bends away from the normal
Emerging ray is parallel to the original but displaced

teach.heading: Core practical: refraction through a glass block
bullets: Place the block on paper; draw its outline and a normal
Shine a ray at different angles of incidence i
Mark the ray in and out, and measure i and r
Plot sin i against sin r: gradient = n
teach.note: Independent variable: angle of incidence; dependent: angle of refraction; controls: same block, same wavelength (single-colour ray). Use a sharp pencil and protractor to ±1°. Safety: ray-box lamps get hot. Expected: a straight line through the origin; gradient about 1.5 for glass.

model.problem: A ray hits a glass block at i = 40° and refracts at r = 25°. Calculate the refractive index.

teach.heading: Finding the angle of refraction
bullets: Rearrange: sin r = sin i ÷ n
Use the inverse sine key
Check that r < i going into glass
teach.note: Show the rearrangement carefully. A frequent error is using the calculator in radian mode. Pupils check that the answer is smaller than the incident angle going into a denser medium.

model.problem: A ray hits glass (n = 1.5) at an angle of incidence of 30°. Calculate the angle of refraction.

practice: A ray hits a plane mirror with an angle of incidence of 25°. State the angle of reflection and the angle between the ray and the mirror surface.
Calculate the refractive index of a material when i = 50° and r = 30°.
A ray enters water (n = 1.33) at 45°. Calculate the angle of refraction.
independent: Core: Draw a ray diagram showing a ray passing through a rectangular glass block, labelling normals, i and r.
Extend: Describe how you would find the refractive index of a glass block and how you would use a graph to improve accuracy.
Stretch: Explain why an object at the bottom of a swimming pool looks closer to the surface than it is.
exit: State the law of reflection.
Explain why a ray entering glass bends towards the normal.
lessons.homework: Complete a practical write-up for the glass-block investigation using a table of results for i = 10°, 20°, 30°, 40°, 50° with your own measurements or sample data.
lessons.send: SEND: use a printed protractor guide and a calculator key sequence card for sin and sin⁻¹. EAL: pre-teach normal, incident, refract. Stretch: derive n = speed in vacuum ÷ speed in material.

lessons.title: Total internal reflection, critical angle and optical fibres
lessons.bigQuestion: How can a thin glass fibre carry a phone call or an internet video across an ocean?
objectives: Explain total internal reflection (TIR)
Use sin c = 1 ÷ n
Describe how optical fibres and endoscopes work
successCriteria: All: state the conditions for TIR
Most: calculate the critical angle
Some: explain how light is guided along an optical fibre and compare fibres with copper cables
lessons.crossCurricular: Medicine: endoscopes; Computing: broadband
lessons.smsc: Moral: using technology for the good of others in medicine and communication

keywords.def: the angle of incidence in the denser medium at which the refracted ray travels along the boundary (c)
all the light is reflected back inside the denser medium
a thin glass or plastic strand that carries light by repeated TIR
outer layer with a lower refractive index than the core

starter: Bismillah. A ray enters glass at 30°. Does it bend towards or away from the normal?
Calculate n when i = 45° and r = 28°.
State the law of reflection.

teach.heading: When light cannot escape
bullets: Light goes from a dense to a less dense medium (e.g. glass to air)
Below the critical angle: refraction and a weak reflection
At the critical angle: refracted ray along the surface
Above the critical angle: total internal reflection
teach.note: Use a semicircular block: aim the ray at the curved side along a radius so it is not bent on entering. Increase the angle of incidence inside the block until the emerging ray skims the surface: that angle is c. Safety: hot lamps; avoid looking into the beam.
cycle: Small angle: most light refracts out, a little reflects
Increase i: refracted ray bends further from the normal
At i = c: refracted ray runs along the surface (90°)
For i > c: all the light reflects inside: TIR

teach.heading: Critical angle calculations
bullets: sin c = 1 ÷ n
Higher n gives a smaller critical angle
TIR happens only from denser to less dense
teach.note: Derive from n = sin i/sin r with r = 90° and sin 90° = 1. Compare glass, water and diamond; ask why diamonds sparkle (a small critical angle means light is trapped and reflected many times).

model.problem: Glass has a refractive index of 1.5. Calculate the critical angle for a glass-air boundary.

teach.heading: Optical fibres
bullets: Core of glass with a lower-index cladding
Light enters and hits the boundary above the critical angle
TIR repeats, guiding light along, even round bends
Uses: endoscopes, broadband, telephone cables
teach.note: Endoscope: one bundle carries light in, another returns the image, so doctors can look inside the body without major surgery. In telecommunications, pulses of light (infrared) carry digital signals. Fibres lose less signal and carry more data than copper wire.

head: Use
Why a fibre is suitable
rows: flexible; carries light and an image without surgery
fast, carries lots of data, little signal loss
light is guided to the tip by TIR

teach.heading: Check: TIR
bullets: Select the best answer
teach.note: Option B reverses the direction. Option C is a common slip: TIR does not depend on colour. Ask for the two conditions.

check.q: Which conditions are needed for total internal reflection?
options: Light going from air to glass at any angle
Light going from glass to air at an angle above the critical angle
Light going from glass to air at an angle below the critical angle
Light going from air to water at 90°
check.why: TIR needs light in the denser medium reaching the boundary at an angle greater than c. Option C gives refraction.

practice: Calculate the critical angle for water (n = 1.33).
Diamond has n = 2.42. Calculate its critical angle and explain why it sparkles.
Explain why a ray in a glass fibre does not escape through the sides.
independent: Core: Describe two uses of optical fibres.
Extend: A ray in glass (n = 1.50) hits the glass-air boundary at 38°, then 45°. State whether it refracts or reflects in each case, giving reasons.
Stretch: An optical fibre has a core with n = 1.52 and cladding with n = 1.48. Calculate the critical angle at the core-cladding boundary and explain why a cladding is better than bare glass.
exit: State the equation for the critical angle.
Explain why TIR cannot occur when light goes from air into glass.
lessons.homework: Draw a ray diagram showing light travelling along an optical fibre and write four labelled steps explaining how an endoscope works.
lessons.send: SEND: diagram with the three cases (below c, at c, above c) to label. EAL: pre-teach critical, internal, cladding. Stretch: compare step-index and graded-index fibres.

lessons.title: Sound waves: hearing range, speed of sound, pitch and loudness
lessons.bigQuestion: How can an oscilloscope help us see the difference between a quiet low note and a loud high note?
objectives: Describe sound as a longitudinal wave needing a medium
State the human hearing range and typical speeds of sound
Interpret oscilloscope traces for pitch and loudness
successCriteria: All: state the range of human hearing and that sound needs a medium
Most: calculate distance using the speed of sound and echoes
Some: calculate frequency from an oscilloscope trace and design a speed-of-sound experiment
lessons.crossCurricular: Music: pitch, loudness; Maths: speed = distance ÷ time
lessons.smsc: Spiritual: the beauty of sound in recitation and the care taken to protect our hearing

keywords.def: region where the air particles are close together, high pressure
region where particles are spread out, low pressure
sound above 20 000 Hz
how high or low a note sounds: depends on frequency

starter: Bismillah. Calculate the speed of a wave with f = 250 Hz and λ = 1.36 m.
Is sound longitudinal or transverse?
Convert 20 kHz to Hz.

teach.heading: How sound travels
bullets: Source vibrates and pushes particles: compressions and rarefactions
Needs a medium: no sound in a vacuum
Faster in solids than liquids than gases
Human hearing: about 20 Hz to 20 000 Hz
teach.note: Bell jar demonstration: sound fades as air is removed. Particles are closer in solids so vibrations pass more quickly. Typical speeds: air about 340 m/s, water about 1500 m/s, steel about 5000 m/s.

teach.heading: Echoes and the speed of sound
bullets: Echo: reflection of sound
d = v × t, but the sound travels there and back
Distance to the wall = ½ × v × t
teach.note: Practical idea: two pupils stand 100 m from a large wall; one claps, the other starts a stopwatch on each echo, timing 20 echoes to reduce error. Alternatively use two microphones connected to a timer. Safety: keep away from roads. Use the 340 m/s value unless the question gives another.

model.problem: A pupil claps and hears the echo from a cliff 0.50 s later. The speed of sound is 340 m/s. How far away is the cliff?
steps: Distance there and back = v × t = 340 × 0.50 = 170 m

teach.heading: Pitch and loudness on an oscilloscope
bullets: Higher pitch means higher frequency: more waves on the screen
Louder means larger amplitude: taller waves
Period from the time base: T = divisions × time per division
f = 1 ÷ T
teach.note: Show traces of a quiet low note, a loud low note and a quiet high note. The vertical axis shows voltage (amplitude), the horizontal shows time. Read off the time for one complete wave.

model.problem: On an oscilloscope, one complete wave takes 4.0 divisions. The time base is set to 2.5 ms per division. Calculate the frequency.

teach.heading: Check: trace comparison
bullets: Compare two traces
teach.note: Option A reverses amplitude and frequency. Ask pupils which feature of the trace is the pitch and which is the loudness.

check.q: Trace B has the same height as trace A but twice as many waves across the screen. Compared with A, the sound in B is...
options: the same loudness and higher pitched
the same loudness and lower pitched
check.why: Same height means the same amplitude, so the same loudness. More waves in the same time means a higher frequency, so a higher pitch.

practice: Calculate the wavelength of a 400 Hz note in air, speed 340 m/s.
A ship's sonar sends a pulse and detects the echo from the sea bed after 0.80 s. The speed of sound in water is 1500 m/s. Calculate the depth.
A trace has a period of 5.0 ms. Calculate the frequency.
independent: Core: State two differences between a loud, low-pitched sound and a quiet, high-pitched sound.
Extend: Lightning is seen, and thunder heard 6.0 s later. Estimate the distance to the lightning (speed of sound 340 m/s).
Stretch: Design an experiment to measure the speed of sound in air, listing the equipment, measurements, calculation and one way to reduce uncertainty.
exit: State the range of human hearing.
Explain why sound cannot travel through a vacuum.
lessons.homework: Write a short explanation of why a space film showing explosions with sound is not realistic, using the idea of a medium.
lessons.send: SEND: give an oscilloscope grid with annotated example traces. EAL: pre-teach amplitude, pitch, echo. Stretch: explain why sound speeds differ in terms of particle spacing.

lessons.unit: Physics 4: Energy resources and energy transfers
lessons.title: Energy stores, transfers, conservation and efficiency
lessons.bigQuestion: Where does the energy go when a light bulb is switched on, and can it ever be destroyed?
objectives: Describe energy stores and transfers
State the principle of conservation of energy
Calculate efficiency and interpret Sankey diagrams
successCriteria: All: name energy stores and transfers in a system
Most: calculate efficiency
Some: draw and interpret a Sankey diagram with correct arrow widths
lessons.crossCurricular: Chemistry: energy changes; Maths: percentages and ratios
lessons.smsc: Moral: avoiding waste (israf) of resources, including energy

keywords.def: a way energy is kept, such as chemical, kinetic or gravitational potential
energy cannot be created or destroyed, only transferred or dissipated
useful energy output ÷ total energy input (× 100%)
spread out to the surroundings, usually as thermal energy

starter: Bismillah. Calculate the power of a device transferring 600 J in 20 s.
Name two renewable and two non-renewable energy resources.
Calculate 18 as a percentage of 24.

teach.heading: Stores and transfers
bullets: Stores: chemical, kinetic, gravitational, elastic, thermal, nuclear
Transfers: mechanical work, electrical work, heating, radiation (light, sound)
Total energy is always conserved
