teach.note: Describe a few systems on the board: a boiling kettle, a falling ball, a speaker. Ask pupils to name the stores and transfers. Energy is conserved, but much becomes less useful thermal energy in the surroundings.

teach.heading: Efficiency
bullets: Efficiency = useful energy output ÷ total energy input
Multiply by 100 for a percentage
Never more than 100%
Wasted energy = input - useful output
teach.note: Say clearly that energy is not 'lost'; it dissipates. Efficiency may also be written using power: useful power output ÷ total power input. Do a quick check: can a device be 120% efficient?

model.problem: A motor takes in 200 J of electrical energy and lifts a load, gaining 150 J of gravitational potential energy. Calculate its efficiency and the energy wasted.

teach.heading: Sankey diagrams
bullets: Arrow width shows the amount of energy
Input arrow splits into useful and wasted arrows
The widths add up to the input
Use a scale, e.g. 1 mm = 1 J
teach.note: Draw a Sankey for a 100 J lamp: 10 J light and 90 J thermal. Ask pupils to draw the arrow widths to scale on squared paper. The input arrow and the output arrows must balance.

model.problem: A kettle transfers 2000 J of electrical energy. 1800 J heats the water and 200 J heats the surroundings. Describe the Sankey diagram and calculate the efficiency.
steps: Input arrow: width 20 mm (1 mm = 100 J)
Useful arrow: width 18 mm (heating the water)

teach.heading: Check: efficiency
bullets: Choose the answer
teach.note: Option A uses the wasted fraction. Option D is an impossible value. Ask how to check the answer is sensible.

check.q: A device wastes 30 J of every 120 J supplied. Its efficiency is...
check.why: Useful output = 120 - 30 = 90 J, so efficiency = 90 ÷ 120 = 75%. 25% is the wasted fraction.

practice: A lamp takes in 60 J and gives out 6 J of light. Calculate its efficiency and the wasted energy.
Name the energy stores before and after a ball is dropped and hits the floor.
Draw a Sankey diagram for a 400 J input with 300 J useful output.
independent: Core: A toaster transfers 1000 J electrically: 800 J heats the bread. Calculate the efficiency.
Extend: A machine is 40% efficient and wastes 90 J. Calculate the input energy.
Stretch: Two light bulbs give the same light. Bulb A has efficiency 8% and bulb B 40%. Compare the energy input needed from each to produce 20 J of light.
exit: State the principle of conservation of energy.
A motor has an efficiency of 60%. Calculate its useful output if the input is 500 J.
lessons.homework: Choose two household devices, identify the energy transfers and draw a Sankey diagram for each using realistic percentages.
lessons.send: SEND: give squared-paper Sankey templates with scales. EAL: pre-teach waste, dissipate, efficient. Stretch: efficiency of energy chains such as power stations.

lessons.unit: Physics 4: Energy resources and energy transfers
lessons.title: Thermal energy transfer: conduction, convection and radiation
lessons.bigQuestion: Why does a vacuum flask keep tea hot for hours?
objectives: Describe conduction, convection and radiation
Explain how to reduce unwanted thermal transfer
Plan an investigation of heat transfer using cooling
successCriteria: All: name the three methods of thermal transfer
Most: explain each in terms of particles or waves
Some: explain how a design reduces all three and plan a fair test
lessons.crossCurricular: Design and Technology: insulation; Geography: weather
lessons.smsc: Moral: caring for the environment through reducing energy waste in homes

keywords.def: transfer of thermal energy through a solid by vibrating particles and free electrons
transfer of thermal energy by the movement of a heated fluid
transfer of thermal energy as infrared waves, needing no medium
a material that is a poor conductor of thermal energy

starter: Bismillah. State two ways to improve the efficiency of a device.
Calculate the efficiency when 45 J of 60 J is useful.
State the speed of infrared radiation in a vacuum.

teach.heading: Conduction
bullets: In solids, particles vibrate and pass energy on
Metals conduct best: free electrons carry energy quickly
Gases and liquids conduct poorly
Trapped air is a good insulator
teach.note: Demonstrate with metal rods coated in wax, heated at one end. Link to why a metal spoon feels colder than a wooden one at the same temperature: it conducts heat away from your hand faster.

teach.heading: Convection and radiation
bullets: Convection: hot fluid expands, becomes less dense and rises
Cooler, denser fluid sinks, setting up a convection current
Radiation: infrared; no particles needed
Dark matt surfaces absorb and emit best; shiny surfaces are poor
teach.note: Show a convection current with potassium permanganate crystals in water over a heat source, or a heater in a room. For radiation ask how the Sun's energy reaches us: through a vacuum, so it is not conduction or convection.
cycle: Fluid is heated at the bottom
It expands and becomes less dense
The warm fluid rises
It cools at the top, becomes denser and sinks
The cycle continues as a convection current

teach.heading: Core practical idea: surfaces and cooling
bullets: Four identical cans: matt black, shiny silver, white, and shiny with a lid
Fill each with the same volume of hot water
Record the temperature every minute for 10 minutes
Plot temperature against time for each can
teach.note: Independent variable: surface colour or finish; dependent: temperature fall over 10 min; controls: starting temperature, volume of water, room, thermometer. Expected result: the matt black can cools fastest as it emits the most radiation. Safety: hot water, scald risk; use a kettle with care and keep spills away from sockets.

model.problem: Explain how a vacuum flask reduces heat loss by conduction, convection and radiation.
steps: Vacuum between the walls: no particles, so no conduction or convection
Silvered (shiny) surfaces: reflect infrared radiation back
Plastic stopper: poor conductor and traps air to reduce convection
Result: the tea stays hot for a long time
model.answer: The flask reduces all three methods of transfer

teach.heading: Reducing unwanted transfers at home
bullets: Loft insulation: traps air, reduces conduction and convection
Cavity wall insulation: stops convection in the gap
Double glazing: trapped air or vacuum reduces conduction
Reflective foil behind radiators reflects radiation
teach.note: Link back to energy efficiency. Ask pupils which measure would be most cost-effective and why: payback time = cost ÷ yearly saving. Check the hinge question on the next section.

check.q: Why is a layer of trapped air a good insulator?
options: Air is a good conductor and convection stops
Air is a poor conductor and cannot circulate easily when trapped
Air is lighter than most solids
check.why: Air is a poor conductor, and in small trapped pockets it cannot form convection currents. The other statements are not the reason.

practice: Explain why metal feels colder than wood at the same temperature.
State how thermal energy from the Sun reaches the Earth.
Explain why the cooling coil of a fridge is at the back and painted black.
independent: Core: Describe how a convection current forms in a pan of water heated from below.
Extend: A householder installs loft insulation costing £400, saving £80 per year. Calculate the payback time and comment on its value.
Stretch: Explain, with reference to particles and electrons, why copper is a better conductor than glass.
exit: Name the three methods of thermal energy transfer.
Explain why shiny surfaces are used on vacuum flasks.
lessons.homework: Design a fair test to compare two different insulating materials around a beaker of hot water. State the variables, equipment and a safety point.
lessons.send: SEND: give a table to complete: method / medium needed / example. EAL: pre-teach insulate, current, trap. Stretch: investigate rate of cooling and Newton's law of cooling qualitatively.

lessons.unit: Physics 4: Energy resources and energy transfers
lessons.title: Work done, gravitational potential energy and kinetic energy
lessons.bigQuestion: How much energy does it take to climb a hill, and where does it go when you roll down?
objectives: Calculate work done using W = Fd
Calculate gravitational potential and kinetic energy
Use conservation of energy to find speed or height
successCriteria: All: use W = Fd
Most: use ΔGPE = mgh and KE = ½mv²
Some: combine GPE and KE in conservation problems
lessons.crossCurricular: Maths: squaring and square roots; PE: energy in sport
lessons.smsc: Spiritual: observing how effort transfers energy

keywords.def: energy transferred when a force moves an object, W = F × d
energy stored in an object due to its height, mgh
energy of a moving object, ½mv²
the unit of energy and work: 1 N m

starter: Bismillah. Calculate the weight of a 5.0 kg bag (g = 10 N/kg).
Calculate the efficiency when 80 J of 200 J is useful.
State the unit of energy.

teach.heading: Work done
bullets: Work done = force × distance moved in the direction of the force
W = F × d
Work done equals the energy transferred
1 joule = 1 newton metre
teach.note: Link to energy transfer: pushing a box increases its kinetic energy or heats surfaces through friction. A common error is using the wrong distance, or a force at 90° to the motion that does no work.

model.problem: A man pushes a box with a force of 50 N for 4.0 m across the floor. Calculate the work done.

teach.heading: Gravitational potential energy
bullets: GPE = m × g × h
Change in GPE when lifted through height h
g = 10 N/kg unless the question gives a different value
teach.note: Lifting a mass needs a force equal to its weight, so work done = mg × h. That is the link between work and GPE. Use a ball lifted onto a table as a visual.

model.problem: A 60 kg climber ascends a 3.0 m wall. Calculate the gain in gravitational potential energy.

teach.heading: Kinetic energy
bullets: KE = ½ × m × v²
Speed is squared: double the speed means four times the KE
Energy in joules, mass in kg, speed in m/s
teach.note: Insist on squaring v before multiplying. Ask pupils: why is speed so important in crash energy? Link to Physics 1 stopping distances.

model.problem: A 1200 kg car travels at 15 m/s. Calculate its kinetic energy.

teach.heading: Energy conservation: falling objects
bullets: A falling object transfers GPE to KE
If drag is ignored: mgh = ½mv²
Mass cancels
teach.note: Do the example and ask: would a heavier ball land faster in a vacuum? (No, mass cancels.) Remind pupils that with air resistance some energy becomes thermal.

model.problem: A ball is dropped from rest from 5.0 m. Ignoring air resistance, calculate its speed just before hitting the ground.
steps: GPE lost = KE gained: mgh = ½mv²

teach.heading: Check: kinetic energy
bullets: Choose the best answer
teach.note: Option A is the common error of doubling KE when speed doubles. Ask pupils to calculate to check.

check.q: A cyclist doubles her speed. Her kinetic energy becomes...
check.why: KE depends on v², so doubling the speed gives 2² = 4 times the KE.

practice: Calculate the work done by a 15 N force moving an object 6.0 m.
Calculate the KE of a 0.50 kg ball moving at 12 m/s.
A 2.0 kg book is lifted 1.5 m. Calculate the gain in GPE.
independent: Core: A 70 kg person climbs 20 stairs of height 0.18 m each. Calculate the work done against gravity.
Extend: A 0.20 kg ball is thrown upwards at 15 m/s. Calculate the maximum height, ignoring air resistance.
Stretch: A 1000 kg car travelling at 20 m/s brakes to rest using a constant 5000 N braking force. Calculate the braking distance and discuss what happens to the energy.
exit: State the equation for kinetic energy.
Calculate the work done when a 40 N force moves a trolley 3.0 m.
lessons.homework: Complete a table of five energy calculations (work, GPE, KE) with units and write one sentence on where the energy goes in each.
lessons.send: SEND: use a formula triangle card and a squared number reminder. EAL: pre-teach gravitational, kinetic. Stretch: explain why braking distance is proportional to v².

lessons.unit: Physics 4: Energy resources and energy transfers
lessons.title: Power as the rate of energy transfer
lessons.bigQuestion: Two students climb the same stairs; why can one of them be more powerful?
objectives: Define power as the rate of doing work or transferring energy
Use P = W ÷ t and P = E ÷ t
Plan an experiment to measure the power of a person climbing stairs
successCriteria: All: use P = E ÷ t
Most: combine W = Fd or mgh with power
Some: plan a stair-climb power investigation and evaluate it
lessons.crossCurricular: PE: fitness and performance; Maths: rearranging
lessons.smsc: Moral: honest measurement, working with a partner safely

keywords.def: the rate of transferring energy or doing work, in watts
one joule per second
energy transferred by a force over a distance
how much per unit of time

starter: Bismillah. Calculate the GPE of a 50 kg student on a 4.0 m balcony.
Calculate the work done when 20 N moves an object 5.0 m.
Convert 3 kW to W.

teach.heading: Power
bullets: Power = work done ÷ time taken
P = W ÷ t or P = E ÷ t
Unit: watt (W): 1 W = 1 J/s
A more powerful device transfers energy faster
teach.note: Compare two motors lifting the same load: both do the same work, but the more powerful one does it in less time. Link to power ratings on appliances (P = IV).

model.problem: A motor lifts a 20 kg load through 2.0 m in 4.0 s. Calculate the power. (g = 10 N/kg)

teach.heading: Power and efficiency
bullets: Useful power output ÷ total power input
Same as energy ratio
Waste power is dissipated
teach.note: Remind pupils that efficiency compares powers equally well because time cancels. A 500 W motor that gives 350 W of useful output is 70% efficient.

model.problem: A pump has an input power of 800 W and lifts water, gaining GPE at 600 J every second. Calculate its efficiency and the wasted power.

teach.heading: Core practical idea: your power on the stairs
bullets: Measure your mass and the vertical height of the stairs
Time how long you take to climb them
Calculate the work: mgh
Power = work ÷ time
teach.note: Variables: independent: speed of climbing or person; dependent: power; control: same stairs. Measure height with a metre rule or from step height × number of steps. Take repeats. Safety: do not run on stairs; stop if breathless. Expect 150 to 300 W for a short climb. Discuss errors: reaction time, not exact vertical height.

model.problem: A 55 kg student climbs stairs of vertical height 3.0 m in 5.0 s. Calculate the power.

teach.heading: Check: power calculation
bullets: Choose the best answer
teach.note: Option A divides the wrong way round. Option C forgets time. Ask for units.

check.q: A machine does 600 J of work in 15 s. Its power is...
check.why: P = W ÷ t = 600 ÷ 15 = 40 W. 9000 comes from multiplying; 0.025 from inverting.

A 2.0 kW heater runs for 5.0 minutes. Calculate the energy transferred.
A motor transfers 3000 J in 20 s. Calculate its power.

Extend: A 60 W lamp is 5% efficient. Calculate the useful light power and the thermal power.
Stretch: A 1500 kg car accelerates from rest to 20 m/s in 8.0 s. Calculate the average useful power.
exit: State the unit of power and what it means.
A 3.0 kW kettle runs for 2.0 minutes. Calculate the energy transferred.

lessons.unit: Physics 4: Energy resources and energy transfers
lessons.title: Generating electricity: fuels, nuclear and renewable resources
lessons.bigQuestion: Which energy sources should a country use to keep the lights on for the next fifty years?
objectives: Describe how electricity is generated in power stations
Compare renewable and non-renewable resources
Evaluate advantages and disadvantages of each resource
successCriteria: All: describe a basic power station and name sources
Most: give an advantage and a disadvantage for each source
Some: evaluate a choice of resource for a given location
lessons.crossCurricular: Geography: energy supply and sustainability; Citizenship: environmental policy
lessons.smsc: Moral: stewardship (khalifah) of the Earth and fairness to future generations

keywords.def: a resource that is replaced as fast as it is used, or will not run out
a resource that will run out, such as coal, oil, gas and uranium
a device that transfers kinetic energy to electrical energy
a rotor turned by steam, wind or water

starter: Bismillah. Calculate the efficiency when 90 J of 360 J is useful.
State the energy transfer in a wind turbine.
State what is meant by a fossil fuel.

teach.heading: How most power stations work
bullets: Fuel releases thermal energy (burning or nuclear fission)
Water boils to steam
Steam turns a turbine
Turbine spins a generator, producing electricity
teach.note: Draw the energy chain. Note that wind, water and tidal power skip the boiler and drive the turbine directly; solar cells produce electricity directly. Geothermal uses hot rocks to make steam.
cycle: Chemical or nuclear energy released as thermal energy
Water heated to make steam
Steam turns the turbine
Turbine turns the generator
Electricity transferred to the grid

teach.heading: Comparing the resources
bullets: Fossil fuels: reliable but release CO₂ and are finite
Nuclear: no CO₂, but produces radioactive waste
Wind, solar, hydro, tidal, geothermal: renewable, no fuel cost
Intermittent supply is a limit for wind and solar
teach.note: Pupils annotate the table with one extra point each from memory, for example wind: no fuel; visual impact; works only when the wind blows. Ask which sources can be switched on quickly to meet demand. Gas and hydro are quick.

teach.heading: Evaluating a choice
bullets: State the context and criteria
Give advantages and disadvantages
Weigh them up and reach a judgement
Use evidence: reliability, cost, pollution, location
teach.note: Use the model as a template for 6-mark answers. Pupils should use connecting words (however, therefore). Do not push a particular view; teach the structure of an evaluation.

model.problem: A remote island needs electricity. Evaluate using wind turbines compared with a diesel generator.
steps: Wind: renewable, no fuel deliveries and no CO₂
Wind: variable supply, needs backup or storage
Diesel: reliable on demand but fuel must be shipped; CO₂ and noise
Judgement: combine wind with storage or a small diesel generator for reliability
model.answer: A mix of wind with backup is likely best: it cuts fuel use but still gives a reliable supply

teach.heading: Check: renewable
bullets: Select the best option
teach.note: Option B is a typical error (nuclear fuel is not replaced). Ask why 'renewable' does not mean 'no disadvantage'.

check.q: Which of these is a renewable energy resource?
check.why: Tidal energy is replenished by the Moon's pull and the Sun. Uranium, gas and coal are finite.

practice: Describe how a coal-fired power station produces electricity.
Give one advantage and one disadvantage of nuclear power.
Explain why solar cells are not suitable as the only source of electricity for a UK city.
independent: Core: Make a table of three renewable and three non-renewable resources with one advantage each.
Extend: Explain why hydroelectric power can respond more quickly to demand than coal.
Stretch: Evaluate whether a country with high sun and little rain should invest in solar farms or in importing gas, giving a reasoned conclusion.
exit: State what is meant by a renewable resource.
Explain why a wind farm may not always provide electricity.
